Mr. President, On behalf of the core group comprising Costa Rica and my country, Qatar, I have the honor to present the draft resolution L28 entitled, "Promotion and the Protection of the Human Rights of Women and Children in Conflict and Post-Conflict Situations, Remedies and Reparation for the Victims." The world today is witnessing an unprecedented number of conflicts, where around 130 armed conflicts age across the globe, a figure that has more than doubled in the last 15 years, according to the ICRC. Recent statistics have shown that the majority of victims of these conflicts are civilian women and children, who are particularly and disproportionately affected by violence and subjected to the most horrific violations of their rights. In almost all armed conflicts, the common factor always being blatant disregard for human rights and IHL rules and principles by conflicting parties, which has had direct repercussions on the lives of women and children. Mechanism to provide justice, remedies, and reparation for those human right inadequate. Protection measures and accountability for gross violations of international human right law and serious violation and abuses of international humanitarian law also fall short of delivering true justice to the victims with silence in the face of widespread impunity. Against this backdrop, the initiative of this timely resolution is an updated call for taking more concrete measures to protect and to promote the human rights of women and children during conflict and post-conflict, and to make their voices and needs remain central to all justice and accountability process. Over the course of three rounds of informal consultations and bilateral encounters, the core group strived to the best with open mind and heart to deal with more than 230 comments received, with sometimes more than 10 different comments for the same paragraph, and the struggle to strike a delicate balance to find common ground and to keep the text constructive, focused, actionable, and consensual one. This is surprising. when it is well known that there are numerous examples of harassment, reprisals, and attacks in developed countries against social movements, youth leaders, migrants, and people of African descent cooperating with the UN system. There has been frequent repression, harassment, and repression of rights of university students and the thousands of people that protest in the streets of these countries and that call for an end of the complicity of their governments with the genocide committed by Israel against the Palestinian people. The Cuban delegation reiterates its rejection of any abuse of human rights mechanisms with goals outside of those of the Council mandate and that go against the Charter of the United Nations. Thank you very much.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cyprus.

Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honour to speak on behalf of the EU Member States that are members of the Human Rights Council. This General Comment has been agreed by the EU as a whole. The EU thanks the Core Group, Hungary, Ireland, Uruguay, Fiji and Ghana for once more presenting this important initiative and for their transparent and inclusive approach during the consultation process, accommodating a broad range of suggestions from States and civil society. The EU expresses its resolute support for the right of everyone, individually and in association with others, to access, communicate and cooperate freely with the United Nations and its mechanisms. Yet reports of intimidation and reprisals continue to persist across all regions. We condemn in the strongest terms all acts of intimidation and reprisals, online and offline, by state and non-state actors. These actions weaken both individuals' and civil society's ability to contribute meaningfully to UN processes. We further condemn the targeting of human rights mechanisms and the deterrent effect this has on those who seek to cooperate with the UN. We appreciate that the text before us highlights the particular challenge of the increasingly transnational nature of acts of reprisals and the chilling effect that fear of retaliation has on individuals and organizations. Many victims of reprisals request anonymity during documentation or refrain from reporting altogether. The true number of reprisals cases is therefore likely to be much higher than what is included in the Secretary-General's annual report. We are further concerned that under-reporting hampers efforts to ensure accountability and to step up prevention efforts. For the reasons presented above, the EU supports the text as presented by the Core Group and calls on all members of the Human Rights Council to join the consensus on this important resolution. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Chile.

Thank you very much, President. Chile thanks the core group made up of Hungary, Fiji, Ghana, Uruguay, and Holland for presenting this draft resolution, which addresses a matter that attacks the very heart of the human rights system, the acts of intimidation and reprisals against those seeking to cooperate or cooperating or have cooperated with the mechanisms and representatives of the United Nations on this matter. The numerous reports from the High Commissioner's Office, special procedures, show persistent patterns of reprisals and intimidation against those cooperating with the system, whether it's through threats, smear campaigns, or prosecutions, or administrative restrictions, and trying to silence victims, human rights defenders, and witnesses. We see a weakening of accountability, and we see hindrance to the work of the Council in meeting its mandate to protect and promote human rights. For this reason, Chile reiterates its categorical condemnation of all forms of reprisals or intimidation, whether it's from state actors or non-state actors. We express our full backing to the efforts of the Secretary-General, the High Commissioner, and the Under-Secretary-General for preventing these cases. In this context, we thank the core group for presenting this updated version of this text. and for having conducted transparent and constructive negotiations. Chile calls upon this Council to adopt this by consensus, reaffirming that cooperation with the human rights system is only possible if we are to ensure the effective protection of those who show their commitment and bravery in doing so. Thank you very much, Mr. President.
Thank you. I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of South Africa.

Mr. President, South Africa wishes to provide general comments in support of resolution L25, which we have co-sponsored. In doing so, my delegation expresses its gratitude to the core group for their openness and flexibility and for incorporating South Africa's proposals. This resolution is important for South Africa, as we may not have been able to take our pride of place here at the Council were it not for the solidarity of civil society, together with supportive member states, which exposed the tyranny of apartheid at the UN. As part of this process, they successfully managed to mobilize the international community to fight what the world ultimately decried as a crime against humanity, which contributed greatly to bringing the apartheid state to its knees. Not only is South Africa a nation born of human rights defenders, but many of our people paid the ultimate price for cooperating with the UN and were subjected to, amongst others, extrajudicial executions. We can therefore always be counted on to defend the right of unhindered access to and communication with the UN. Accordingly, South Africa is concerned about the intimidation and reprisals being undertaken against individuals and groups for cooperating with the UN, including the unique challenges faced by those in situations of armed conflict or under foreign occupation. We are similarly concerned that the very special procedure mechanisms that individuals and groups are meant to cooperate with are themselves the subject of intimidation and reprisals. This is particularly the case for those seeking to draw attention to the genocide in Gaza, which has been brought to the fore by the range of special procedure mechanisms, including a special procedure on the OPT, together with several individuals and groups. The imposition of sanctions undermines the integrity of the UN human rights system. As such, South Africa concurs with the High Commissioner that attacks against international institutions and their personnel must cease. The resolution before us recognizes these imperatives. As member states, we must therefore work resolutely to ensure that individuals and groups who engage with the UN, together with the special procedure mechanisms with whom they interact, can collectively undertake their respective responsibilities without fear in a safe and enabling environment. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, Japan appreciates the efforts of the core group behind the draft resolution, L25, namely Hungary, Fiji, Ghana, Ireland, and Uruguay, in preparing this draft resolution. Japan recognizes that contributions and engagement by civil society actors are crucial to promote and protect human rights, both in national and international contexts. Especially, civil society's meaningful participation in this Council is integral to ensuring that we have fruitful discussions. As highlighted in the report of the UN Secretary-General submitted to this session, we are deeply concerned that the civil society actors Cooperating with the United Nations face increasing obstacles and harassment, including transnational repression, which prevent them from operating freely. As a traditional co-sponsor of this resolution, Japan values the strengthened language in both the preambular and operative parts of the text. We believe those improvements acutely reflect the revolving nature of reprisals, including the misuse of legislation, transnational repression, digital surveillance, and gender-based harassment. We also welcome the emphasis on prevention, accountability, and the sharing of good practices by states and UN actors. Furthermore, Japan again emphasizes the importance of ensuring a safe, free, and inclusive environment for cooperation with the United Nations by civil society actors, both online and offline. States bear the primary responsibility to prevent, investigate, and ensure accountability for acts of intimidation or reprisals, and we en- we encourage continued constructive dialogue and transparency on these issues. We reiterate our firm commitment to protecting civ- civic space so that civil society actors can cooperate freely with the United Nations. Taking all of the above into consideration, Japan strongly hopes that this draft resolution will be adopted by consensus. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Netherlands.

Thank you, Mr. President. The Kingdom of the Netherlands would like to join others in thanking the core group for their work in presenting this resolution. Support to human rights defenders and civil society is a long-standing priority of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, as they play a vital role in informing and shaping UN decisions, enhancing accountability and promoting inclusive dialogue, all of which are essential for the UN's effectiveness. Yet, reports of intimidation and reprisals remain a serious concern in all regions. These acts undermine human rights and fundamental freedoms, considerably impede the Human Rights Council's ability to fulfil its mandate effectively, and strike not only at those who courageously advocate for human rights, but also at the very foundations and proper functioning of the United Nations system. The Kingdom of the Netherlands strongly condemns these unacceptable and unjustifiable practices of reprisals. The Kingdom of the Netherlands believes we have a collective responsibility to take action to respond to these acts and recognises the invaluable contribution of our civil society partners. The core group took a balanced and consensual approach throughout the whole negotiation process to address key issues of concern. The strong and balanced outcome deserves the support of this Council. We therefore urge all Council members to join consensus on this resolution and send a clear message of the importance that the HRC attaches to civil society engagement with the UN system. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Costa Rica.

Thank you, President. Costa Rica thanks the group proposing this draft resolution. In the opinion of my delegation, this text is one of the most important outcomes of the session. Multilateral work that we are all working in here must be able to be undertaken in a safe environment, free of threats and intimidation, in which all actors, including civil society and human rights defenders, can work in a respectful climate, yes, but fully exercising their rights to freedom of speech and expression. the freedom of assembly and association as well. No one should fear cooperating with the UN, nor working with the UN. Costa Rica wishes to underscore two very relevant matters. First, that there be recognition that special procedures mandate holders designated by this Council are ever more subjected to attacks as a result of their functions, including repressive measures against them and the deterrent effect that that has on the willingness of people and groups to cooperate with the UN, their representatives and mechanisms. Second, my country welcomes those who have proposed this for including the issue of transnational repression in PP23. This has caused deaths, including Nicaraguans in Costa Rica. Also very worrisome are the acts of oppression committed by states or agents under their effective control. This causes damage, intimidates, and silences human rights effectors or political opposition or refugees or others abroad through digital means, physical means, and other means, including through spying programs. Costa Rica reaffirms its unbreakable commitment to the protection of all individuals that cooperate with the UN system in the area of human rights. My country calls upon all states to ensure that cooperation with the international mechanisms happen without fear of reprisals in a climate of respect and accountability and transparency. those raising their voice for human rights. It is only with them that we can strengthen the legitimacy and the efficacy of the multilateral system. Costa Rica is pleased to be a co-sponsor of this text. We reiterate our full support for L25, and we encourage it to be adopted without a vote. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Colombia.

Thank you. President Colombia welcomes the draft resolution on cooperation in the United Nations. and its mechanisms in the area of human rights. We thank Hungary, Fiji, Ghana, and Uruguay for the presentation, and we wish to underscore the importance of this topic. The multilateral system can only meet its mandate if the voices of victims, human rights defenders, and experts can express themselves without fear of reprisal. We, Colombia, fully and strongly condemns all acts of harassment, reprisals, sanctions, against those cooperating with the United Nations. The cases that we have recently seen from indigenous defenders and to Special Rapporteurs are unacceptable examples of the manner in which there are efforts to silence those who raise their voice for justice and truth. In the same way, we are deeply concerned over the trend of extending these reprisals to those cooperating with other universal or regional accountability bodies. established under international law, such as the International Criminal Court. Attacks, reprisals against their staff and personnel and against those supporting their activities, including their investigations and rulings, seek not just to obstruct justice, but also to undermine the fight against impunity. We must remember that behind every report, every witness, every investigation, and every decision or activity, we have the victims. They are the most forgotten when states resort to reprisals against those who cooperate with the United Nations, defending those who are defending rights. is to defend the heart itself of multilateralism. For this reason, Colombia calls upon all Member States to respect and protect the work of the mechanisms of this Council, of the independent experts and rapporteurs, and other mechanisms such as international courts. President, the credibility of the Council and the entirety of the international human rights system hinges on our ability, our collective ability, to ensure that no individual fears cooperating with the United Nations or with international judicial bodies. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

Thank you. I have been informed by the Secretariat that there are no PBIs for this draft proposal. I now give the floor to members of the Council who wish to make explanations of vote before the vote on draft proposal L25. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

Mr. President, China supports the work of the UN human rights mechanisms in accordance with their mandates and their constructive dialogue and cooperation with Member States. We oppose all acts of intimidation and reprisal against those who cooperate with the UN, its representatives, and mechanisms. China is a country with the rule of law, where everyone is equal before the law. Violators of the law must be held accountable and face consequences. Any illegal or criminal acts carried out under the guise of human rights must be punished in accordance with the law. We oppose the abuse of UN mechanisms to shield and protect criminal elements. With a cooperative and constructive attitude, China has actively participated in consultations on the draft resolution, and we have raised many legitimate concerns and proposed amendments both orally and in writing. We thank the core group for their attention and taking them on board. Regrettably, The draft resolution remains unbalanced and does not fully respect the legitimacy of countries' sovereign legislation and the lawful punishment of criminal acts. Certain content exceeds the mandate of relevant UN mechanisms. In view of the above, we will disassociate ourselves from consensus on draft resolution L25, and we request our position to be registered. Thank you.

I don't see any other request for the floor. Is there a request for a vote? I see none. May I take it that draft proposal L.25 may be adopted without a vote? It is so decided. Thank you. Mr. President, it's an honor for me to present to the Human Rights Council on behalf of Brazil and the African Group the draft resolution L22 entitled "A World of Sports Free from Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance." The persistence of racist incidents in sports requires us to be vigilant and step up our actions aimed at eliminating those scourges. Brazil and the African Group would like to take this opportunity to reiterate the importance of continuing to address this critical issue and to follow up on the regional consultations organized by the OHCHR last semester. We hope this draft resolution will contribute to advancing international cooperation and further strengthen our collective commitment to combating racism in sports from a human rights perspective. We would like to thank all delegations and the civil society for the constructive discussions during the informal consultations. Mr. President, we are pleased to inform that the draft resolution has garnered a significant number of co-sponsors across different regional groups. We trust this resolution, as in previous years, will receive the strong support from this Council and be adopted by consensus. Thank you.

Thank you. I have been informed by the Secretariat that there are 15 additional co-sponsors. And I will give the floor to members of the Council who wish to make general comments. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cuba.

Thank you, President. We thank the delegations of Brazil and Ghana on behalf of the African Group presenting L22. Cuba reaffirms its commitment to sport free of racism, racial discrimination, religion or belief-based discrimination, xenophobia, or other forms of intolerance or related forms of intolerance. We can support and will continue to contribute to the implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action because of its key role in international efforts to fight racism and racial discrimination. We agree with that expressed in the draft resolution regarding the potential for sport to promote values such as respect, dignity, diversity, tolerance, justice, and social inclusion. Cuba rejects the political manipulation of sport, the transgression of the Olympic values, and the stealing of sporting talent. We support the efforts of the High Commissioner's Office to support within its mandate the national efforts to strengthen or rather to bring capacity building for states and other actors, including sports professionals in preventing and fighting racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and other related forms of intolerance in sport. For the aforementioned reasons, Cuba supports draft resolution L.22. We call for the Council to adopt it by consensus. Thank you.
I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Benin.

President, thank you, President. President, Benin condemns and will always condemn firmly all forms of racism, xenophobia, or intolerance, whether it is on the sports field, in the seats, or online, because sports are called upon to create an area of tolerance, mutual respect, freedom, discipline and fraternity between athletes. But from this viewpoint, when racism appears in national and international sports events, it is the very spirit of sports that is undermined. on the Treaty on the Eradication of All Forms of Racism, we are resolutely committed to fully implementing the Durban Plan of Action, and Benin is making human rights a pillar of its sports policies, notably working towards integration of the module on tolerance and non-discrimination into school sports and physical education. and within sports federations to fight all forms of discrimination based on gender or religion. As a member of this Council, it is our duty to continue to promote sports exempt of any racial discrimination, xenophobia or intolerance associated with it, because sport is only true to itself if it reflects our common humanity, and this is why Benin strongly hopes that this proposal will be adopted by consensus. Thank you.
The English representative of Ethiopia.

Thank you, Mr. President. As I said, Ethiopia extends its sincere appreciation to Ghana and Brazil for their leadership in advancing this important initiative. We commend their efforts to facilitate an inclusive and constructive process leading to the presentation of this timely draft resolution L22. Ethiopia reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the elimination of all forms of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance, including within the field of sport, which represents one of the most powerful tools for promoting equality, solidarity and mutual understanding across cultures and communities. We believe that sport must be a safe and inclusive space for all. and that is transformative power can only be fully realized when it is free from hatred, exclusion and discrimination. In this regard, we welcome the resolution's comprehensive approach, particularly it is emphasized on ensuring accountability for racially motivated acts in sport, promoting inclusive representation and advancing zero tolerance policies alongside education and awareness raising to foster a culture of respect, fairness and inclusion. We further underscore the importance of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, which remains a foundational framework in the global fight against racism. The resolution rightly draws up this legacy while also integrating the role of sport in achieving the goals of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, particularly those related to peace, equality and social inclusion. Mr. President, Ethiopia reaffirms its strong support for both the spirit and substance of this draft resolution, and expresses its sincere hope for its adoption by consensus. as a demonstration of our collective commitment to the principle of dignity, equality and non-discrimination. In conclusion, Ethiopia calls upon all members of the Human Rights Council to join us in supporting the consensual adoption of this vital resolution, thereby reaffirming our collective commitment to combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance in sport. I thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bolivia.

President, we thank, we appreciate and hail the work undertaken by Brazil and Ghana on behalf of the African group. Bolivia agrees that sport, more than a competition, is a universal language that can unite people beyond borders, beyond creed and color. However, we also recognize with concern that racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and other related forms of intolerance continue to be present in stadia, in sports bodies, and in the daily life of many athletes. The Human Rights Council, through this draft resolution, will reaffirm the fundamental principle that all individuals have the right to participate in sport without discrimination whatsoever, in step with the values and instruments governing human rights around the world. The draft invites member states to strengthen their public policies, laws, and programs, and educational programs aimed at eradicating all forms of racism in sport, ensuring effective sanctions, and fostering accountability. Silence in the face of discrimination is also a form of complicity. Further, the draft resolution contributes to efforts to empower women and girls that face multiple forms of exclusion and violence in sports and environments. It aims promoting their full participation is not merely a matter of equity, but also justice. We appreciate that in the operative paragraphs, there is an invitation of governments and other relevant bodies to consider the possibility of allocating part of the revenue from sports events to the promotion, inclusion, and participation of persons that have been excluded from sport. Bolivia supports. and co-sponsors, L22, we invite the honorable Council to adopt it by consensus. Thank you kindly.
The representative of Kenya.

Thank you, Mr. President. As a globally recognized nation renowned for its excellence in athletics and long distance running, and a proud co-sponsor of this resolution, We fully welcome the importance of this resolution in combating racism within sport in spirit and substance. Kenya's athletic legacy offers authentic ground to emphasize how sport can unite communities, foster equality and serve as a tool against discrimination. Mr. President, Kenyan runners, many from historically marginalized or rural areas, exemplify how equal opportunity and talent identification can empower individuals and build national pride independent of racial or ethnic distinction. It is worth noting that I come from a region commonly referred to as the home of champions, an area that continues to produce world-class athletes such as Eliud Kipchoge, Faith Kipyegon, and David Rudisha, reflecting the nation's role in demonstrating sports as a universal language that transcends race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic background. Kenya has developed several policy and legal frameworks that address discrimination, governance and ethics within sports, reflecting our commitment to fairness, equality and safeguarding in athletics and sports, including the Sports Act and the Kenya Academy of Sports Safeguarding Policy. The resolution's recognition of sport as a national driver for states towards the realization of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development resonates with Kenya's Vision 2030 and its commitment to youth empowerment, education, and gender equality through sport. In welcoming consensus on this resolution, we reaffirm that sport should represent the power of diversity and resilience beyond ethnicity or race. I thank you.
